query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A dual-channel ab initio framework that independently computes lattice heat transport (via anharmonic phonon Boltzmann transport with explicit disorder-induced scattering) and electronic transport (via a Kubo–Greenwood formalism from DFT) will predict the thermal conductivity of low-oxygen HfNbTaTiZr with an improvement of approximately 25–50% in error over traditional single-parameter (Debye temperature based) models. This methodology will accurately capture the comparable lattice and electronic contributions at temperatures below 200 K and yield reliable total conductivity estimates between 300 and 1200 K.
generation.material_initial_state: Concentrated, defect-free bulk crystalline HfNbTaTiZr with minimal oxygen contamination (<1 wt.% oxygen).
generation.intervention: Apply a combined DFT-based computational approach that separately calculates lattice contributions using anharmonic phonon Boltzmann transport (with explicit treatment of disorder-inducing scattering mechanisms) and electronic contributions using a Kubo–Greenwood-based method.
generation.conditions: Temperature range spanning low (<200 K, where lattice and electronic contributions are comparable) to high (300–1200 K) temperatures on controlled, low-oxygen specimens.
generation.structural_mediator: Atomic-scale disorder including variations in interatomic force constants and anharmonic effects that influence phonon lifetimes, as well as detailed electronic band structure effects.
generation.mechanism: By decoupling lattice and electronic transport mechanisms, the method avoids oversimplifications inherent in single-parameter models. This separate treatment allows explicit capture of scattering processes and anharmonicity for phonons and precise electronic structure effects, leading to reduced overall predictive error.
generation.predicted_outcome: The model will yield thermal conductivity predictions that reduce error by ~25–50% compared to existing Debye-temperature-based estimates, accurately reflecting separate lattice and electronic contributions at low temperatures and matching overall conductivity measurements at higher temperatures.
generation.baseline: Existing predictive methods that conflate lattice and electronic contributions using averaged parameters (such as a single Debye temperature) applied to ideal, defect-free crystals.
generation.boundary: The approach is expected to perform reliably only in well-controlled, defect-free or low-oxygen HfNbTaTiZr samples; its accuracy may diminish in samples with significant oxygen contamination or other defects that introduce additional scattering not accounted for in the model.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative error improvement could vary with experimental conditions; precise separation and measurement of the lattice and electronic contributions below 200 K remain experimentally challenging.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform temperature-dependent thermal conductivity measurements on high-purity, low-oxygen HfNbTaTiZr samples. Utilize techniques capable of disentangling lattice and electronic contributions at low temperatures (e.g., complementary measurements using thermal diffusivity and Seebeck coefficient assessments) and measure overall thermal conductivity in the 300–1200 K range.
measurements: Total thermal conductivity (via standard thermal transport measurements)
Separate lattice contribution (e.g., via phonon lifetime measurements using inelastic neutron or X-ray scattering)
Electronic contribution (via Seebeck coefficient measurements or other electronic transport characterizations)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the dual-channel model fails to achieve at least a 25% reduction in predictive error relative to traditional Debye-temperature based approaches, or if independent experimental measurements of lattice and electronic contributions at low temperatures deviate by more than ±25% from the model predictions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Options for sustainable clean energy include advanced power generation systems that have the potential to drastically reduce the emission of greenhouse gases. These advanced systems are often required to operate under harsh conditions to optimize efficiency, which poses several challenges for the available materials. An example of advanced power system is one that is associated with fusion energy [1] . Beyond traditional fission-based systems, fusion reactors not only promise nearly unlimited clean energy, but also avoid the generation of long-life radioactive waste produced in fission devices. One remaining challenge is that of materials, which can withstand extreme conditions of radiation, temperature, and stress, with long-term steady properties for the power plant to be economically viable [2] – [4] . High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are defined as equimolar or nonequimolar single- and multiphase solid solutions, depending on the number and type of principal/secondary metallic elements with the configurational entropy greater than 1.61 R , (where R is the gas constant) ( [1] , [2] ). The minimization of the Gibbs free energy by increasing the configurational entropy results in the formation of a single- or multiphase solid solution, such as body-centered cubic (BCC) ( [3] ), face-centered cubic (FCC) ( [4] ), and/or hexagonal close-packed solid-solution phases ( [5] ) instead of intermetallic compounds ( [6] ). Moreover, the random distribution of multiple elements with different atomic radii leads to a severely distorted lattice with variations in the interatomic distances along the crystallographic direction of the unit cells ( [3] ). These features, in turn, contribute to desirable mechanical properties, such as high hardness, strength, ductility, and softening resistance at room temperature (RT) and elevated temperatures ( [3] ).

High entropy alloys have excellent wear resistance, so they have great application prospects in the fields of wear resistance and surface protection. In this study, the wear resistance of the FeNiCrCoCu high entropy alloy coating was systematically analyzed by the molecular dynamics method. FeNiCrCoCu high entropy alloy was used as a coating material to adhere to the surface of a Cu matrix. The friction and nanoindentation simulation of this coating material were carried out by controlling the ambient temperature. The influence of temperature on its friction properties was analyzed on five aspects: lattice structure, dislocation evolution, friction coefficient, hardness, and elastic modulus. The results show that with the increase of temperature, the disorder of the lattice structure increases, which leads to an increase of the tangential force and friction coefficient in the friction process. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The response of atoms to cluster or order in alloys offers deep insights to the microstructural behavior. This trend is particularly important for multi-component alloys, because the ordering can drive the system to various microstructural states, such as crystalline or intermetallic solids, from the disordered FCC ( A1 ), BCC ( A2 ), or HCP ( A3 ) conditions. In Al x CrCoFeNi, the Al content can influence the final structural configuration [6] [23] [24] [25] [26] [27] due to the larger atom size, compared to other constituents, which considerably changes the lattice ordering. When the mole fraction of Al <0.3, a single-phase A1 is observed, and a single-phase A2 is found for Al >1.17, while a two-phase ( A1 + A2 ) for 0.3 ≤ Al ≤1.17 is reported [24] [26] . Polymorphism, which describes the occurrence of different lattice structures in a crystalline material, is a critical phenomenon in materials science and condensed matter physics. Recently, configuration disorder was compositionally engineered into single lattices, leading to the discovery of high-entropy alloys and high-entropy oxides. For these novel entropy-stabilized forms of crystalline matter with extremely high structural stability, is polymorphism still possible? Here by employing in situ high-pressure synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction, we reveal a polymorphic transition from face-centred-cubic ( fcc ) structure to hexagonal-close-packing ( hcp ) structure in the prototype CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy. The transition is irreversible, and our in situ high-temperature synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction experiments at different pressures of the retained hcp high-entropy alloy reveal that the fcc phase is a stable polymorph at high temperatures, while the hcp structure is more thermodynamically favourable at lower temperatures. As pressure is increased, the critical temperature for the hcp -to- fcc transformation also rises.

Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure [1] – [3] . These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C [4] , [5] . Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm 3 ) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added [6] – [13] . High entropy alloys (HEAs) are a new class of metallic materials composed of multiple principle elements in equal or near-equal atomic proportions [1] , [2] . They have been receiving significant research interest owing to their exceptional mechanical and functional properties; see, e.g., refs [3] – [5] . Among various reported HEAs, the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi (Cantor alloy) [6] is a popular and important prototype of HEAs based on 3d transition metals. Within a wide range of temperature below its solidus, it usually forms a chemically disordered solid solution in face-centered cubic (fcc) structure at ambient pressure [6] – [9] . A unique mechanical characteristic of the Cantor alloy is an enhanced strength-ductility combination with decreasing temperature, while maintaining outstanding fracture toughness at cryogenic temperatures, which was demonstrated to be closely related to the formation of nano-twins and stacking faults in deformation [7] , [10] – [15] . Furthermore, due to the irreversible pressure-induced phase transition from the fcc to the hexagonal close-packed (hcp) lattice, the presence of the hcp structure was recently observed at ambient conditions [16] – [18] . Key components in magnetic fusion reactors, such as the divertor or the plasma-facing materials (PFMs), are required to have stringent properties including low activation, high melting point, good thermomechanical properties, low sputter erosion, and low tritium retention/codeposition. They must operate at high temperature (≥1000 K) for long durations (>10 7 s), without failure or extensive erosion while exposed to large plasma heat and an intense mixture of ionized and energetic neutral species of hydrogen isotopes (D and T), He ash (fluxes, >10 24 m −2 s −1 ), and neutrons ( [1] ). Tungsten (W) is the leading PFM candidate because of its high melting temperature, low erosion rates, and small tritium retention. These advantages are unfortunately coupled with very low fracture toughness characterized by brittle transgranular and intergranular failure regimes, which severely restrict the useful operating temperature window and also create a range of fabrication difficulties. Metallic alloys containing multiple principal alloying elements, which are known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [1] – [3] , have attracted extensive research interest in recent years with many studies focused on their microstructure, mechanical properties, and underlying deformation mechanisms [4] – [6] . For example, as a new class of structural materials, certain face-centered cubic ( fcc ) alloys, in particular CrCoNi-based HEAs, have been shown to possess improved strength and exceptional damage tolerance, especially at cryogenic temperatures [7] , [8] .

decision.trend: Earlier work on refractory HEAs typically used simplified analytical and semi‐empirical models—varying atomic masses and force constants, temperature‐dependent phonon calculations based on Debye temperatures, or DFT-derived elastic properties applied to estimate conductivity. These approaches largely assumed ideal, defect‐free bulk crystals and, by design, mixed lattice and electronic transport contributions. Although these methods captured some overall trends, experiments (e.g., showing comparable lattice and electronic contributions below 200 K and low total conductivity at high temperatures in oxygen‐containing samples) reveal that the current analyses do not fully address the underlying atomic‐scale complexity.
decision.unsolved: A method that quantitatively separates lattice and electronic heat transport—capturing the full temperature dependence and effects of atomic-scale disorder (including low-level oxygen contamination)—remains to be developed. In particular, isolating and quantifying the individual scattering mechanisms without relying on coarse approximations such as a single Debye temperature is an open challenge.
decision.lever: Develop a combined ab initio framework that separately computes lattice transport via anharmonic phonon Boltzmann transport (with explicit treatment of disorder-induced scattering) and electronic transport via a Kubo–Greenwood-based formalism directly from DFT electronic structure. This approach eliminates reliance on single-parameter models (like a Debye temperature) and directly incorporates atomistic complexity.
decision.why: Such a method naturally follows the trend: while prior approaches used averaged properties and convolved contributions, a dual-channel, first-principles simulation would account for the separate scattering mechanisms, leading to a quantifiable improvement (anticipated error reduction of 25–50% compared with earlier estimates) across the full temperature range (from below 200 K up to 1200 K). Decisive experimental falsification would be possible by comparing separately measured lattice and electronic contributions at low temperatures (where they are comparable) and the overall conductivity at high temperatures, particularly on low-oxygen specimens.
